title: After 70 Years of Excavation, Ancient Sardis Earns UNESCO World Heritage Status
summary: For seven decades, archaeologists have returned to Sardis in western Turkey, peeling back layers of Lydian, Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman history. This summer, their persistence was rewarded: Sardis was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, recognizing its extraordinary cultural continuity and the groundbreaking archaeological work that has revealed it. The site is legendary. As the capital of Iron Age Lydia, Sardis is where the first coins were minted under King Croesus, whose wealth became proverbial. Its strategic location between the Mediterranean and Anatolia made it a crossroads of East and West. "Because it was not overbuilt by a modern city, Sardis gives you a really long history, from the Bronze Age to basically today," said Annetta Alexandridis, associate director of the excavation. Since 1958, the Harvard-Cornell Expedition has meticulously uncovered this history. Early efforts reconstructed a monumental bath-gymnasium complex and the largest synagogue in the ancient world, setting a standard for archaeological restoration. More recent digs have revealed a gold refining workshop, a Persian-era garbage pit, and a sanctuary plaza that required 15 years to excavate. The project is also a training ground for new archaeologists and a model for community engagement. "From the very beginning, there's been a desire to communicate results and make the work legible to tourists and locals," noted Benjamin Anderson, a Cornell professor. The UNESCO designation not only honors this legacy but also confronts a complicated past. Early 20th-century excavations removed artifacts under questionable circumstances, including a column now at the Met. Sardis thus embodies the evolving ethics of archaeology — from exploitation to stewardship. As Anderson put it, the long-term commitment has generated "a critical mass of data" that now allows the city's story to be told through its material remains, not just ancient texts.
why_it_matters: Sardis isn't just a pile of old stones — it's a record of how people lived, traded, and worshipped for 3,000 years. Its UNESCO listing shows how careful, honest archaeology can right the wrongs of past treasure hunts and teach us that history belongs to everyone, not just museums in faraway countries.

background_read: Sardis is one of the great layered cities of the ancient world. Lydian kings like Croesus (whose name became a byword for wealth) ruled a kingdom that straddled trade routes between the Aegean Sea and the Anatolian plateau (the vast Asian part of modern Turkey). Lydians were the first people in history to use standardized gold and silver coins around 600 BCE, a revolutionary idea that spread quickly.

After Lydia fell to the Persians, Sardis became a regional capital under successive empires — Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and finally Ottoman. That long occupation means the site is like a layer cake of civilizations, with palaces, temples, shops, and houses built on top of one another.

The Harvard-Cornell Expedition began digging in 1958, when archaeological methods were much less scientific. Over the decades, the team has become a model for long-term, interdisciplinary research, combining excavation with architectural conservation, geology, and community outreach. They even run a field school where students learn cutting-edge techniques.

UNESCO World Heritage status (awarded by a United Nations organization that protects sites of outstanding universal value) brings international recognition but also responsibility. The controversial removal of the Met column in the early 1900s reflects a time when Western museums often took antiquities without proper permission. Today, ethical archaeology emphasizes leaving artifacts in their context and involving local communities.

Sardis's new listing could boost cultural tourism and funding, but it also reignites debates about repatriation — whether objects like the Met column should be returned. Benjamin Anderson, a Cornell professor involved in the project, notes that the long-term data now lets archaeologists write the city's history from its material remains, not just from ancient texts that often left out ordinary people.

perspectives.description: UNESCO status boosts tourism and funding, bringing economic benefits and a sense of cultural pride to the local region. The site's careful restoration sets a standard for other projects and proves that patient, multi-generational research can pay off.

The removal of the column to the Met represents a painful chapter when Western archaeologists took treasures without consent. Critics argue that true ethical stewardship should involve repatriation demands, not just acknowledgment. The UNESCO label might also attract mass tourism that could damage fragile remains.

Sardis's value lies in its continuous occupation — from Bronze Age to Ottoman — making it a rare case study in urban evolution. The excavation's shift from focusing on kings to studying everyday garbage and workshops shows how archaeology itself has changed, becoming more interested in ordinary lives and long-term processes.

With 'critical mass' of data, digital modeling and DNA analysis could soon tell the story of Sardis's people — what they ate, where they came from. Future decisions about returning artifacts like the Met column will test whether UNESCO listing can truly push archaeology toward justice and not just celebration.
